blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Video generation models are now strong enough to tell stories [ 58 , 33 , 51 , 45 ] , and agents that plan shots, track characters, and check results keep multi-shot videos consistent across scenes [ 60 , 26 , 62 , 86 , 68 ] .
Live streaming, games, and world models need a different kind of generator: autoregressive (AR), few-step models that stream long videos in real time and accept new prompts while they play [ 77 , 28 , 74 , 6 , 40 , 23 , 19 , 47 ] .
These generators have no agent.
Their memory is the key/value (KV) cache: an attention sink that keeps the first frames [ 65 , 74 ] and a short window of recent frames.
Older content is forgotten, and what is kept is the model’s own output, so a wrong face or a lost object is copied forward [ 28 , 11 ] .

blocks.en:
Adding an agent is hard because agents think slowly and real-time video cannot wait.
A live session imposes four constraints that offline agent systems do not face: (C1) the future is unknown, so memory for a shot must be ready before its prompt arrives; (C2) there is no length limit, so GPU memory must stay constant; (C3) the deadline is hard, so the video never waits for memory construction: planning, drawing, and prefilling must stay hidden, and once a prompt arrives only a quick choice among prepared memory is affordable; (C4) there is no rollback, so played shots cannot be repaired.
Existing video agents rely on what a live session lacks: they read the whole script (C1), plan each shot while generation waits (C3), and inspect and regenerate failed shots (C4) [ 60 , 26 , 55 ] .

现有的视频代理依赖于直播会话所缺少的内容:他们阅读了整个剧本(C1),在一代人等待(C3)时计划每个镜头,检查并再生失败镜头(C4)[60,26,55].

blocks.en: We present Agentic LongLive , an asynchronous agentic memory that gives real-time AR generators a long-term memory without slowing them down ( Fig. 1 ). Asynchronous memory: a memory agent runs on its own GPUs and commits the memory for shot i i before prompt i i is revealed, and an auxiliary GPU prefills it into the generator’s KV cache, so the agent’s time is hidden behind generation. Open-loop entity memory: the agent reads only revealed prompts, never the video, so video errors are not written back. It keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene, composes them into a global image 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and a shot memory 𝐌 \mathbf{M} that enter the frozen generator as attention sinks, and appends text cards of the entities a prompt names. Learning what to remember: before the next prompt is known, the agent must choose which entities to draw. We train a small language model for this with reinforcement learning (RL), using a hindsight reward whose image term is calibrated using downstream video outcomes.

blocks.en:
We also build LongStory-Online, 25 stories (857 shots, about 150 minutes) with hidden annotations, where prompts are revealed one shot at a time and every shot is generated exactly once.
On LongLive-2.0 [ 6 ] , Agentic LongLive improves persistent state, protagonist identity, and location on scene changes by 26 to 45 points, adding about 1% generation time on H100, and streams faster than real time on one 8 × \times B200 node in BF16 (34.3 FPS).
Its image quality stays flat over 14-minute stories, its identity gains carry over to two few-step MiniMax-H3 generators [ 45 , 43 ] , with LongLive-H3 also in real time on B200 (1.45 × \times ), and RL lets an 8B planner replace the 35B planner.
We contribute: • an asynchronous agentic memory system that hides agent latency behind real-time generation with constant GPU memory and no length limit, to our knowledge the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent; • an open-loop two-layer memory as attention sinks of a frozen AR generator, with entity cards in the prompt; • an RL recipe with a video-calibrated reward that teaches a small LLM what to remember, and the LongStory-Online benchmark. Related work is reviewed in App. A .

blocks.en:
DiT ranks generate video ( Fig. 2 ). Auxiliary ranks run a decoder that streams latents through the VAE, like the asynchronous decoder of LongLive-2.0 [ 6 ] , and a prefill worker that holds a copy of the DiT weights, encodes memory images with the frozen VAE, and computes their sink K/V, each on its own GPU. Agent ranks host a vision–language model that plans and checks, and an image model that draws memory images.
Data flows one way: from the agent to the prefill worker, then to the DiT, and on to the decoder for display.
The agent never waits for decoding, and memory K/V are ready before the shot that uses them (GPUs per role in Sec. 3.1 ).

Memory for shot i i is prepared while shot i − 1 i-1 is generated, between the reveals of p i − 1 p_{i-1} and p i p_{i} ( Fig. 2 ).
Version 0 is committed as soon as it is drawn, even if it fails its check, so checks do not cause lag ( 𝐆 \mathbf{G} follows a stricter rule, App. B ), and is prefilled at once.
If time remains, the agent may redraw an image that its check flags. The new version replaces the committed one only if it passes and scores no lower.
At the boundary, the DiT swaps in the newest fully prefilled version as a whole, without waiting for one in progress, so no shot mixes two versions. If no new version is ready, it keeps the previous memory (lag, Sec. 2.1 ).
The agent thus has one shot’s time per memory (budget in App. B ), and as the video never waits, the generator alone sets the throughput.

blocks.en: 2.3 Two-layer memory
blocks.zh: 2.3 双层内存

blocks.en:
Every person, object, and scene is an entity with a text state and images ( Fig. 3 a): views for people and objects, and an empty plate for scenes.
After a prompt is revealed, the agent draws new or changed entities.
Since the next prompt is unknown (C1) and played shots are final (C4), memory holds the current belief about each entity.
Images keep only attributes that persist across shots (identity, clothing, dirt, damage, assembly) and leave pose and action to the next prompt.
Each state records its source, so a contradicting later prompt can revoke it (App. C ).

blocks.en:
Generators cannot read an entity database, so the agent composes two images for them ( Fig. 3 b).
The global image 𝐆 \mathbf{G} shows the protagonist and long-term key objects in their current state on a plain studio backdrop, and is refreshed when one of them changes.
The shot memory 𝐌 i \mathbf{M}_{i} shows the current scene and its active entities, one per shot. 𝐆 \mathbf{G} thus carries identity and state but no place, which is left to 𝐌 \mathbf{M} and the prompt.
Both are composed with entity images as references rather than redrawn from text, so an object keeps its look across shots.
Entity images are drawn or edited in the background and checked once.
The rules for refining 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and 𝐌 \mathbf{M} are in App. B .

blocks.en: 3.1 Setup
blocks.zh: 3.1 设置

blocks.en:
Every method sees one prompt per shot, generates each shot once, and never reads future prompts.
Regeneration and best-of- N N are not allowed, but a baseline keeps its own closed-loop mechanisms.
LongStory-Online has 25 stories, 857 shots, and about 150 minutes of video: nine stories written by hand (211 shots) and sixteen LongStory-Hard stories designed by an LLM with states accumulated by code (646 shots).
Stories have more entities than memory slots, long absences and revisits, persistent changes (clothing, dirt, damage, assembly), and prompts that overturn earlier inferences.
Each shot has a hidden annotation of entities, persistent states, and location, frozen before any method was run.
Prompts are terse , like real user input: a place or person is described once, and later prompts use names or “back in the kitchen”.
blocks.zh:
每种方法每发一发都看到一发即发,产生一发即发,从不读取未来的即发即发.
不允许再生和最佳N型,但基准保持自己的闭路机制。
Long Story-Online有25个故事,857个镜头,以及大约150分钟的视频:由手写出9个故事(211个镜头)和由LLM设计的16个由代码积累的状态(646个镜头).
故事比记忆槽有更多的实体,长时间的缺席和再审,持续的变化(衣物,污垢,损坏,组装),并促使推翻先前的推论.
每一枪都有隐藏的注释,说明实体,持续状态和位置,在任何方法运行之前被冻结.
提示是terse, 就像真正的用户输入:一个地方或个人被描述一次, 之后提示使用名字或“回到厨房”。

blocks.en:
LongLive-2.0 [ 6 ] shares our backbone and keeps its built-in memory: sinks on the first chunk of the video and of each shot, and a KV window carried across shots.
Four open AR models on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, Self-Forcing [ 28 ] , CausVid [ 77 ] , Causal-Forcing [ 89 ] , and Rolling Forcing [ 40 ] , run one rollout per story with the prompt switched at each shot.
Self-Forcing breaks down within minutes, as in its official code (83% of its shots have severe artifacts), so we do not rank it.
On MiniMax-H3 [ 45 ] , we test two few-step chunked-AR generators: RAVEN [ 43 ] and LongLive-H3 .
We distill LongLive-H3 from MiniMax-H3 by causal distribution matching distillation (DMD) [ 76 ] on prompts alone. It generates video and audio in chunks of about 0.7 s, each attending to the text, the first chunk, and the two previous chunks (App. C ).
Without memory, each 8 s shot is generated from its prompt alone. A second baseline carries K/V across shots as LongLive-2.0 does (App. C ).
The non-real-time systems StoryMem [ 83 ] and StoryEngine [ 60 ] , an offline variant of ours, SkyReels-V2 [ 5 ] , and all baseline adaptations are in App. F .
blocks.zh:
LongLive-2.0 [6] 分享了我们的骨干,并保持了内在的记忆:在视频和每一镜头的第一块上下沉,一个KV窗口横跨镜头.
Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B上有4个公开的AR型,自强[28],CausVid [77],Causal-Forcing [89],和滚出Forcing [40],每出一出一出,每出一出一出,每出一出即时切换.
自强在几分钟内就崩溃了,正如其官方代号(83%的镜头有严重的文物),所以我们不给它排级.
在MiniMax-H3 [45]上,我们测试了两台几相块式AR发电机:RAVEN [43]和LongLive-H3.
我们从MiniMax-H3中分馏出LongLive-H3,仅通过在提示上通过因果分布匹配分馏(DMD)[76]. 它以约0.7 s 的块来生成视频和音频,每个块负责文字,第一个块,以及前两个块(App. C.).
没有记忆,每个8 s的镜头都是由它的快取产生. 第二个基线是K/V横穿镜头,如LongLive-2.0(App.C.)。
非实时系统 StoryMem [83]和StoryEngine [60],我们的一个离线变体,SkyReels-V2 [5],所有基线改编均在App.F.

blocks.en:
A VLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash), different from every model of the real-time agent and of RL training, compares four frames of each shot with its annotation: State (persistent attributes correct), Identity (the visible protagonist matches its description), and Location (on scene changes). Same protagonist compares each shot whose plan shows the protagonist with the method’s first shot of it (0 if the protagonist is missing). Revisit rates whether a return shows the same place as the last visit and counts only returns where both shots are at their planned place [ 60 ] .
We also report VBench imaging quality [ 29 ] and the share of shots with severe artifacts.
Framing, imaging drift [ 40 ] , and ArcFace face identity (MIR [ 60 ] ) are in App. E and H .
Re-judging agrees on 92–96% of decisions. As the same model also wrote the Hard stories, a second judge from another family (GPT-5.5) re-judged 14 runs and confirms 87 of the 94 significant comparisons, with no sign flip (App. E ).
Automated-metric differences quoted in the text are differences of table entries, significant unless noted (a story-clustered bootstrap 95% interval excludes zero).

blocks.en: 3.2 Main results
blocks.zh: 3.2 主要成果

blocks.en:
On LongLive-2.0, our system and the built-in memory share the generator and the prompts, so the comparison isolates memory.
The full system improves all five consistency columns ( Tab. 1 ). State accuracy rises by 26.3 points, and revisit consistency from 15.0% to 55.4%.
Imaging quality also improves and, unlike with the built-in memory, does not decay over a story ( Fig. 6 ).
The cost is about 1% generation time on H100 ( Sec. 3.3 ). Sections 3.4 and 3.5 separate the contributions of memory images, scene routing, entity cards, and the RL planner.
blocks.zh:
在"LongLive-2.0"上,我们的系统与内置内存共享生成器和提示,因此比较隔离了内存.

Without memory, severe artifacts are rare (0.5% and 0.9%) because each shot starts from noise, so errors cannot carry over.
Carrying K/V across shots, as LongLive-2.0 does, also raises identity (RAVEN 61.0 % → 91.2 % 61.0\%\rightarrow 91.2\% ), but each shot then continues the previous one: location falls to 20–26%, errors accumulate along the story (9.4% and 11.6% severe artifacts), and our full system leads it by 63–67 location points.
Memory or entity images given as references instead of sinks cause more severe artifacts, and entity references need a prompt rewrite after each prompt (App. C ).

blocks.en:
MiniMax-H3 is a partial exception to C3: its text comes first in the sequence, so encoding the chosen pictures and one forward pass stay on the critical path (1.0–1.2 s per shot with the release code, 0.5 s after optimization), while planning and drawing stay hidden.
Half of its release time is decoding after the whole shot. Faster DiT kernels and decoding split over the same four B200s bring a shot to 6.4 s (30 FPS), and streaming the decoder on a fifth GPU to 5.5 s (34.7 FPS, 1.45 × \times ), with the first frames after 1.5 s.
The agent on the other three GPUs has every update ready at the 8 s playback pace.
On H100, generation needs eight GPUs (7.1 s per shot), and an agent on H100 misses two thirds of the deadlines (App. B ).

blocks.en:
We train Qwen3-8B on 56 generated stories and test it on LongStory-Online, which other authors and models wrote ( Tab. 4 ).
Remembering more in text does not give better videos.
With a text-only reward, the planner recalls the most facts and keeps the most returning entities, yet its videos have the lowest identity of all planners, 14.1 points below the 35B planner.
Its 𝐌 \mathbf{M} contains only 19.2% of the entities that the next shot shows.
With the video-calibrated image term of Eq. 2 , this share rises to 67.4%, and image memory gains 3.6 state and 7.0 identity points over the 35B planner.
SFT on the same stories, the warm start of RL, brings the 8B planner level with the 35B planner, so the gain comes from RL.
Using the calibrated weights without rendering 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and 𝐌 \mathbf{M} during training keeps most of it ( + 2.5 +2.5 state, + 5.0 +5.0 identity).
RL also keeps far more returning entities in the entity bank (83.9% vs . 7.1% after 8+ absent shots, Fig. D1 ) and draws them once they return, whereas the 35B planner retires entities that leave the story.
Entity cards already state the tracked facts in text, so on top of them the RL planner’s lead shrinks to + 0.5 +0.5 state, + 1.8 +1.8 identity, and + 3.2 +3.2 revisit points, none significant (App. C ). In the full system, RL thus lets one 8B model select members and write entity states in place of the 35B planner.

SFT在同一故事上,RL的温暖起步,与35B的策划者一起带来了8B的规划者级别,所以收益来自于RL.
在训练期间使用不渲染出G\mathbf{G}和M\mathbf{M}的校正权重保持了大部分(+2.5+2.5状态,+5.0+5.0身份).
RL在实体银行中还保留了更多的回归实体(83.9%对7.1%的8+缺席镜头后,图D1),并在回归后取出,而35B的策划者则将离开故事的实体退休.

blocks.en:
Because the agent only decides what the generator sees and leaves the generator unchanged, we also test it on robot video models (App. G ).
In robotics, a camera that stays close to an object for longer than the context window loses the rest of the scene.
On the robot video model of Long-WAM [ 27 ] , the original model then turns to a different scene. An observation-based variant of our memory, which stores the initial scene and an object crop in the sink, keeps both and brings them back ( Fig. 7 ).
This variant differs from the agent of Sec. 2 : its memory pictures are frames that the camera has already shown, not drawn images. For long robot tasks (App. G ), it also reads the generated video (closed loop) and sees each instruction one segment before it plays, because a robot acts in one continuous scene whose state depends on what was generated.

在机器人学中,一个与物体相近的时间长于上下文窗口的相机会失去其余的场景.

这个变体不同于 Sec. 2 的代理:它的内存图片是相机已经显示的帧,而不是所绘制的图像. 对于长相机器人任务(App. G),它也读取所生成的视频(闭环),并在播放前看到每个指令的一个段,因为一个机器人在一个连续的场景中行动,其状态取决于生成的内容.

blocks.en: 4 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 4 结论

blocks.en:
We presented Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for real-time long video generation.
A memory agent that reads only revealed prompts keeps entity memory and commits memory images that an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator’s attention sink, so the video never waits for memory, and RL teaches a small planner what to remember.
On LongStory-Online, this improves state, identity, and place consistency of LongLive-2.0 at about 1% extra generation time and streams faster than real time in BF16 on one B200 node. Image quality stays flat over 14-minute stories, and the identity gains carry over to two MiniMax-H3 generators, with LongLive-H3 also in real time.
blocks.zh:
我们介绍了Agentic LongLive,一个实时长相视频生成的同步代理内存.
一个只读出提示的内存代理人保存了实体内存并承诺一个辅助GPU预先将内存图像填充到发电机的注意力下沉中,因此视频从不等待内存,而RL则教给一个小规划师什么是记得的.
在LongStory-Online上,这提高了LongLive-2.0在一个B200节点上的状态,身份,并将一致性放在大约1%的额外生成时间和流比实时快. 图像质量在14分钟多的故事中保持平平,身份增益会延续到两台MiniMax-H3发电机,而LongLive-H3也实时.

blocks.en: Appendix A Related Work

blocks.en:
Diffusion Forcing [ 4 ] and CausVid [ 77 ] make video diffusion causal.
Self Forcing [ 28 ] and its successors [ 11 , 40 , 43 ] close the train–test gap with self rollouts and few-step distillation.
MAGI-1 [ 53 ] , SkyReels-V2 [ 5 ] , Krea Realtime [ 34 ] , APT2 [ 38 ] , and StreamDiT [ 32 ] scale this up.
To run without a length limit, these models keep a fixed window of recent frames and an attention sink [ 65 ] .
Rolling Sink [ 35 ] keeps this cache close to what the model saw in training, without retraining, so rollouts stay stable far beyond the training horizon.
LongLive [ 74 ] adds a frame sink and KV re-caching for prompt switches.
LongLive-2.0 [ 6 ] adds multi-shot sinks and parallel inference, and LongLive-Plug [ 75 ] distills few-step and long-video LoRAs once and plugs them into other models of the same backbone family.
Other works pack or route longer context [ 84 , 3 , 63 ] , split the cache into sink, archive, and working banks [ 82 ] , or retrieve earlier frames by the current prompt [ 30 ] .
In all of them, memory lives inside the generator and is built from its own frames (closed loop).
Our memory lives outside the generator and is written by an agent from the prompts alone.

blocks.en:
Agentic storytelling systems write scripts, draw keyframes, and repair shots with VLM feedback [ 60 , 26 , 62 , 86 , 25 , 55 , 71 , 59 , 68 ] .
The closest, StoryEngine [ 60 ] , keeps structured entity states and canonical references.
All of them run offline: they see the full script and can select or regenerate shots.
Concurrent works bring agents closer to streaming.
AgiWorld [ 15 ] links a planning agent and a video world model through a shared spatial memory.
Wizard [ 64 ] controls a real-time game world model with a VLM agent that turns instructions into programs over scene geometry.
AgiWorld does not report real-time operation, and Wizard’s agent edits scene geometry and a symbolic game state, not image memory.
To our knowledge, ours is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent: the video never waits for the agent, and the whole system streams faster than playback.
Other methods keep memory inside the model.
They carry keyframes or long context across shots [ 83 , 44 , 20 , 66 ] or index past frames by pose and time [ 67 , 79 , 36 ] , so their memory comes from generated pixels.
Reference-to-video models [ 41 , 17 , 13 , 45 ] inject a fixed set of reference images.
We instead decide what to store and update it during the session, and our memory images can serve as references.
blocks.zh:
代理讲故事系统编写脚本,绘制键框,并用VLM反馈来修复镜头[60,26,62,86,25,55,71,59,68].
最接近的"史地英克"[60],保持了结构化的实体状态和教条参照.
他们都跑出线外:他们看到完整的脚本,可以选择或再生镜头.
同时期的作品使得代理商更接近于流出.
AgiWorld [15] 通过共享空间内存将一个规划代理和一个视频世界模型连接起来.
Wizard [64] 使用VLM代理控制一个实时游戏世界模型,将指令转化为程序而超越场景几何.
AgiWorld不报告实时操作,而Wizard的代理编辑了场景几何和象征性的游戏状态,而不是图像记忆.
据我们所知,我们的是第一个拥有由LLM代理保存的文本和图像内存的实时视频生成器:视频从不等待代理,整个系统流速快于回放.
其他方法将记忆保存在模型内部.
它们携带键框或长上下文横跨镜头[83,44,20,66]或按姿势和时间来索引过去帧 [67,79,36],因此它们的内存出自所生成的像素.
参考到视频模型 [41, 17, 13, 45] 注入了一套固定的参考图像.
相反,我们决定在会议期间储存和更新什么,我们的记忆图像可以作为参考。

blocks.en:
Robot systems run a slow planner beside a fast controller [ 1 , 57 , 46 , 56 ] , and LLM agents overlap thinking with waiting [ 10 , 9 ] .
Our slow agent instead must commit versioned memory to a separate real-time generator before a deadline.
LLM agents also learn what to store [ 49 , 70 , 8 , 88 , 72 , 78 ] , and RL tunes prompts for image and video models [ 21 , 61 , 31 , 7 ] with learned judges [ 39 , 69 , 22 ] .
We combine the two.
One LoRA-tuned planner writes the structured memory and the text that the frozen generator reads, and its image reward is calibrated on real videos.

机器人系统在快速控制器旁边运行一个慢编程器[1,57,46,56],LLM代理与等待[10,9]重复思考.
我们的慢代理必须在最后期限之前将版本内存输入单独的实时生成器.
LLM代理也学会了什么可以存储[49,70,8,88,72,78],而RL调子则会与有学问的法官[39,69,22]为图像和视频模型提供提示 [21,61,31,7].
我们把两者结合起来。

blocks.en:
DiT FPS is the number of frames divided by denoising time, excluding VAE decoding, as in LongLive-2.0 [ 6 ] . End-to-end FPS divides frames by wall-clock time including decoding, memory prefill, shot-boundary swaps, and waiting. The real-time factor is video seconds over wall-clock seconds. Overhead is the relative increase in wall-clock time over the base generator on the same hardware, prompts, and video length.
Each method is warmed up and loaded once. Events (start and end of each DiT chunk, end of each decode, memory commit, prefill done, boundary swap) are timestamped after cuda.synchronize , and all numbers come from one timing log per run.
DiT throughput varies by ± \pm 1–2% across GPUs, so overheads within ± \pm 2% are treated as noise.
The H100 timing runs on LongLive-2.0 have no entity cards, which the agent writes off the critical path.

On one 8 × \times B200 node (180 GB each), we keep the story, harness, and GPU layout of Tab. 2 (DiT 1, auxiliary 2, agent 3) and reveal each prompt at playback pace (every 10.54 s), as a live user would, instead of when the previous shot finishes.
Each cuDNN attention call matches FlashAttention-2 to one or two BF16 rounding steps, but whole videos diverge as with any kernel change, so all quality numbers on LongLive-2.0 and on the chunked-AR MiniMax-H3 generators use the evaluated BF16 path (the bidirectional generators of Tab. B4 run in FP8).
With BF16 weights, cuDNN attention, a compiled VAE decoder, and decoding overlapped across shots, LongLive-2.0 streams at 34.1 FPS (1.42 × \times ) and the full system at 34.3 FPS with every update in time ( Tab. B1 ). Memory never stalls the video (wait 0.00 s).
The agent is about 1.6 × \times faster than on H100 (RL plan 2.3–3 s instead of 3.5 s, one image 0.8 s instead of 1.7 s). In this live run, version 0 is ready 5.7 s after a prompt on average (p95 7.8 s, against 10.54 s). With a stand-in generator at the same pace, an agent on H100 GPUs has 34 of 39 updates ready in time ( Tab. B3 ). A fourth agent GPU is an option for longer prompts.

blocks.en:
Table B1 lists the configurations behind Tab. 2 , measured in one session per GPU type on the shots of the timing runs (LongLive-2.0: shots 2–40 of the 40-shot story, LongLive-H3: the 20 full-system shots of the MiniMax-H3 timing runs, after a one-shot warm-up). Its release times are within 1% of Tab. 1 . Table B2 checks quality on the same prompts and seeds with a blind pairwise judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash sees two frames of each shot from both versions in random order and prefers one on detail, realism, and overall, with a sign test over shots) and with no-reference metrics. No optimized path differs significantly from the release under the judge. MUSIQ and sharpness of the final LongLive-2.0 path are 3–7% lower, a shift of the size these metrics also show between paths that the judge cannot tell apart. LongLive-2.0: attention dominates the DiT, so FlashAttention-4 (H100) or cuDNN attention (B200) gives most of the gain. The release decodes the last chunk of each shot after the DiT finishes. Decoding it while the next shot starts removes this tail without changing a bit, and a compiled decoder keeps the decoder GPU ahead of the DiT. One H100 stays below real time even so. LongLive-H3: half of the release time is decoding after the rollout. The fast runtime keeps the model, sampler, and random draws and changes only the kernels (FlashAttention-4 on the KV cache’s layout, a fused QKV GEMM, compiled elementwise operations, BF16 all-reduce with sequence parallelism, and no per-step host synchronization). Decoding runs clip by clip as soon as its latents exist, and a fifth GPU for the decoder streams the first frames 1.5 s after the prompt instead of at the end of the shot.
Memory adds 0.5–0.7 s per shot, mostly encoding its pictures, which the agent could do when it commits them ( encoded at commit ). Per frame, LongLive-H3 needs 3.9 × \times the computation of Wan2.2-5B (83 vs . 21 TFLOP), so it is real time only with more GPUs. Agent at H3’s pace: Tab. B3 drives the live agent with a stand-in generator at the measured shot times. With the agent on B200 GPUs, every update is ready at the 8 s playback pace. Without pacing, faster generation leaves less time and one-shot lag appears, so prompts are revealed at playback pace. With the agent on H100 GPUs, version 0 takes 8–9 s, so most updates arrive one shot late.

blocks.en:
Few-step distillations of MiniMax-H3 that keep its bidirectional attention generate a whole 8 s shot at once, so a shot is shown about 7 s after its prompt instead of 1.5 s for the streamed LongLive-H3. With the same inputs, a blind judge prefers FastH3-Omni over the 50-step model on 71 of 108 shots.
We timed two public ones with reference input, FastH3-Omni with 8 steps [ 16 ] and Pika-H3-Flex with 6 steps [ 50 ] , on one 8 × \times B200 node with the requests of the offline H3 variant (2–6 references per shot). Both need FP8 weights and half-size references to stay near 8 s per shot (BF16 with full-size references: 12.4 and 11.4 s).
Their sequence parallelism runs on 4, 7, or 8 GPUs (56 attention heads), so the generator takes the whole node, and the agent runs on three GPUs of a second node, which exchanges prompts, pictures, and videos with it over the network (about 0.05 s per shot).
With our memory, both generators keep pace with prompts revealed every 8 s ( Tab. B4 ). With at most three memory pictures, a shot takes 6.6 s (FastH3-Omni) and 7.5 s (Pika-H3-Flex), and 38–40 of 40 shots use the newest memory. A shot above 8 s at the client does not delay the next one, as the generator then waits less for its prompt.

The router is the agent’s LLM (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, thinking off, temperature 0).
Its input lists the locations of the committed 𝐌 \mathbf{M} images, each with the name and description the agent wrote for that scene entity from prompts up to p i − 1 p_{i-1} , the location of 𝐌 i − 1 \mathbf{M}_{i-1} , and the full prompt p i p_{i} . The output is constrained to one of the names or NEW.
The system prompt reads: “For every location that earlier shots were filmed in, the memory keeps a picture. … If it takes place in one of the known locations, whether it continues in the previous shot’s location or returns to an earlier one, answer with the exact name of that location. If it takes place in a location that is not in the list, answer NEW. Judge by the physical setting the camera shows, not by which characters or objects are mentioned.” It was written once and not changed after seeing any decision, and nothing in the router is fitted to LongStory-Online.
A recalled 𝐌 \mathbf{M} is written right after 𝐆 \mathbf{G} , attends to 𝐆 \mathbf{G} , uses its source prompt as text, and the video starts 8 frames later, as for a regular 𝐌 \mathbf{M} .
On an H100 the call takes 0.06–0.12 s.
The auxiliary rank keeps [ 𝐆 , 𝐌 loc ] [\mathbf{G},\mathbf{M}_{\text{loc}}] prefilled for every known location (at most eight), so a recall only swaps blocks. This gives bit-identical video to prefilling at the boundary, which would cost 0.87 s per recall.
The router keeps 𝐌 i − 1 \mathbf{M}_{i-1} on 69% of shots, recalls on 17%, and drops on 14%.
Against the hidden annotations of the 832 shot boundaries of LongStory-Online, it injects an 𝐌 \mathbf{M} of the wrong place 19 times (scene gate: 84), an 𝐌 \mathbf{M} of the right place 696 times (gate: 568), and recalls the right place on 94% of the returns whose location is in memory.
The keyword scene gate of Tab. 3 kept 𝐌 i − 1 \mathbf{M}_{i-1} when the opening sentence named its location or shared 20% of content words with the opening of p i − 1 p_{i-1} , and otherwise injected only 𝐆 \mathbf{G} . Shared words such as “back” or “still” made it keep the old place on many returns and changes.

blocks.en:
MiniMax-H3 generates audio and video from a sectioned prompt.
Before any run, each terse prompt is converted once into this format by Gemini 3.8 Flash from that prompt alone and a few story-level constants (the protagonist’s name and voice, the music): one continuous 8 s shot with an opening phrase (shot size, place, where the protagonist is), the action in timeline order with 0–2 short spoken lines, a soundscape, and the music.
The conversion keeps every fact of the terse prompt and adds no appearance, clothing, colour, layout, or prop detail, so the H3 prompts stay as terse as the originals.
All H3 rows, with and without memory, use the same H3 prompts, and the routing decisions of the H3 rows are made on them.

MiniMax-H3从分节的提示生成音频和视频.
在任何运行前, 双子座 3. 8 将每秒提示转换为此格式 单从这个快讯和几个故事层次常数(主角的名字和声音,音乐):一个连续8 s的镜头,并带有一个开口语句(镜头大小,位置,主角所在),行动时间顺序为0–2短口语行,一个音景和音乐.
转换时会使特斯的每一个事实都保持了快活,并且不添加外观,衣着,颜色,布局,或道具细节等,因此H3的提示会像原作一样保持特斯.
所有H3行,有和没有内存,都使用同为H3的提示,H3行的路由决定都在上.

blocks.en:
We obtain LongLive-H3 from MiniMax-H3 by causal distribution matching distillation (DMD) [ 76 ] , with the chunking and few-step schedule of RAVEN [ 43 ] .
The frozen, bidirectional MiniMax-H3 serves as the real-score teacher.
The student is a LoRA of rank 128 on the frozen backbone, and a second rank-128 LoRA serves as the fake-score model, trained by flow matching on the student’s own rollouts. The student is trained with the normalized DMD surrogate, and fake-score and student updates alternate 5:1 after 50 fake-score-only warm-up updates.
Training uses prompts only, without real video or audio: 1,024 original single-shot prompts from SMD-H3-T2VA-100K and 256 multi-shot prompts that we rebuilt from SMD.
Training clips have 124 frames at 1344 × \times 768 and 24 fps with jointly generated 32 kHz stereo audio, i.e . 37 video latents and 207 audio latents per channel. Each clip is split into eight chunks, seven of 5 video latents (about 0.7 s) and a 2-latent tail, with the audio split at the same boundaries.
Attention is block-causal: each chunk attends to the text, the first chunk as a sink, the two previous chunks, and itself, and earlier chunks are fed as clean context at clock 0.999.
We train on 32 GB300 GPUs with a global batch of 64 (2 per GPU), learning rates of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} for the student and 10 − 5 10^{-5} for the fake-score model, and EMA decay 0.99. The released checkpoint is the EMA after 200 student updates (1,000 fake-score updates).
At inference, LongLive-H3 takes 3 steps per chunk and generates 8 s shots (192 frames), longer than its training clips.
With a KV cache that reproduces its chunked sampler, a shot takes 50.2 s on one H100 (116 s on A100), and all quality results use this one-GPU path. Table 1 times it on four H100s with tensor parallelism ( Appendix B ).
RAVEN generates 1376 × \times 768 as released, with 4 steps per chunk.

Without memory, every MiniMax-H3 shot is a separate rollout from its prompt. The second baseline carries K/V across shots as the built-in memory of LongLive-2.0 does, with the mechanism of our sink: the first latent frames of the story’s first shot (a global sink) and the last latent frames of the previous shot are written as one clean chunk after the new shot’s text, so their K/V are recomputed under the new prompt (LongLive’s K/V re-cache [ 74 ] ). RAVEN carries four global and six recent frames (1 s, its K/V window). LongLive-H3, which holds the whole model on one 80 GB GPU in the quality runs, carries one global and two recent frames, the size of our memory chunk. The carried frames end eight video frames (1/3 s) before the new shot, as in LongLive-2.0’s multi-shot format, the shot starts at 2 s, as with our memory chunk, and prompts, seeds, and everything else equal the rows without memory.
Carried K/V raises identity over no memory (RAVEN 61.0% → \to 91.2%, LongLive-H3 58.2% → \to 76.0%, both ∗ ), though less than our full system (96.8–98.0%), but shots continue the previous one: location on scene changes falls to 20–26% (85–86% without memory), and revisits do not improve.
Severe artifacts also accumulate along the story (RAVEN 1.6% of shots 1–10 and 14.9% after shot 20, LongLive-H3 3.6% and 17.5%), mostly colour distortion or corrupted frames, as each shot continues frames that the generator produced under another prompt. With our memory, which comes from the agent rather than from the video, they stay flat along the story (3–6%).

All arms use the same H3 prompts, the same two video seeds, and the same memory stream of the 35B planner, routed by the same LLM router on the H3 prompts (the right 𝐌 \mathbf{M} on 642 of 832 boundaries, against 696 on the terse prompts). Since H3 places text at the start of the sequence, memory K/V depend on the prompt and are computed after it arrives ( Sec. 3.3 ). We compare three ways to pass memory. Sink: on keep, [ 𝐆 , 𝐌 i − 2 , 𝐌 i − 1 ] [\mathbf{G},\mathbf{M}_{i-2},\mathbf{M}_{i-1}] , on recall, [ 𝐆 , 𝐌 loc ] [\mathbf{G},\mathbf{M}_{\text{loc}}] , and on drop, [ 𝐆 ] [\mathbf{G}] , as one clean chunk after the text at 0, 0.25, and 0.5 s, with the shot starting at 2 s. Reference: the H3 Ref2VA transformer with LongLive-H3’s weight update receives the same routed pictures as references, and a fixed template wraps the shot prompt in H3’s reference-prompt sections, with no extra LLM call. Entity references: the same transformer receives up to six committed entity images (one of them the newest plate of the routed place) and the shot prompt rewritten by Qwen3.6-35B-A3B into H3’s full-reference format, without 𝐆 \mathbf{G} or 𝐌 \mathbf{M} . The rewrite takes 6.7 s on one H100 after the prompt, which C3 rules out.
Against our full system (seed 0), entity references reach the same state and identity and a higher revisit ( + 8.2 +8.2 ∗ ), but lower same protagonist ( − 20.3 -20.3 ∗ ), location ( − 13.8 -13.8 ∗ ), and framing ( − 21.8 -21.8 ∗ ) and 11.2 ∗ points more severe artifacts, as shots often open on one of the pictures and then jump into the scene. Passing only the foreground tokens of each entity view brings location back to 83.5% but leaves severe artifacts at 12.4%. Sink memory instead composes the agent’s choice into two prefilled images, whose content the RL planner learns.

The full-system rows (sinks in Tabs. 1 and C1 , references in Tab. C1 ) use the memory stream of the RL planner (training seed 0, the stream of the full system on LongLive-2.0) with the same LLM scene router run on the H3 prompts, and append the same entity cards as on LongLive-2.0 at the end of the description section of each H3 prompt, before the sound sections. The image-memory rows use the 35B planner’s stream with the same router and no cards. MiniMax-H3 encodes the whole prompt (no 512-token window).
All rows use video seeds 0 and 1000 and are compared with the same seeds of the same backbone without memory, with both arms of a story on one GPU type, so every difference is paired by story and seed.

blocks.en:
Sinks need no causal attention. MiniMax-H3 packs the text, the condition images, and the generated video into one sequence on a shared time axis (40 positions per second). Condition rows stay clean and only the video is denoised. Ref2VA places each reference one position after the previous one and starts the video right after the last. For a sink, we move the memory pictures to 0, 0.25, and 0.5 s and the video to 2 s, as on LongLive-H3, and replace the per-picture prompt lines by one sentence saying that the pictures are frames of earlier shots and that the shot starts after a cut. Rows and computation equal those of Ref2VA references, but the pictures are attended to at every denoising step instead of being prefilled once, and memory can change only between shots.
With the per-picture lines of the LongLive-H3 prompts, Pika-H3-Flex often opens on the memory pictures, and the judge prefers the single sentence on 45 of 54 shots.

辛克人不需要因果关注. MiniMax-H3将文本,条件图像,生成的视频打包成共享时间轴上的一个序列(每秒40个位置). 条件行保持干净,只有视频被去名. 参考文献2 VA将每个参考位置放在前一个位置后,然后在后一个位置后立即开始视频. 对于一个水槽,我们将内存相片移到0,0.25和0.5 s,视频移到2 s,就像LongLive-H3上一样,并用一句来取而代之的是:相片是早期镜头的帧,镜头从剪接后开始. 行与计算等同于Ref2VA参考文献,但图片在每个去诺步骤时都会被处理,而不是被预先填充一次,而内存只能在镜头之间变化.
以"长活-H3"提示的平相线为例,皮卡-H3-Flex经常在记忆相片上开口,评委更喜欢在54发中45发上单句.

𝐆 \mathbf{G} shows its members on a plain light-grey backdrop, which covers 70% of its tokens. MiniMax-H3 generators attend to every sink token in every chunk and read this backdrop as a place: with the whole 𝐆 \mathbf{G} , the judge describes a studio or plain backdrop on 36–52% of the new-place shots, where routing injects 𝐆 \mathbf{G} alone, and on 10–15% of the shots with [ 𝐆 , 𝐌 ] [\mathbf{G},\mathbf{M}] (seed 0).
We therefore keep only the foreground of 𝐆 \mathbf{G} . When 𝐆 \mathbf{G} is committed, the agent masks it with the union of a salient-object matte (BiRefNet [ 87 ] , threshold 0.5) and a colour key for smooth, unsaturated, bright regions connected to the image border. The mask is fitted to the video like 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and pooled over the 32 × 32 32{\times}32 -pixel cell of each token, and a token is kept, at its original ( t , h , w ) (t,h,w) position, if at least 10% of its cell is foreground (30% of the tokens on average). Backdrop tokens are never written, and the caption of 𝐆 \mathbf{G} drops its sentence on the backdrop. The mask takes under 0.5 s per 𝐆 \mathbf{G} before the prompt, and nothing else changes.
With only this change ( Tab. C3 ), foreground 𝐆 \mathbf{G} gains 20.1 ∗ (LongLive-H3) and 26.4 ∗ (RAVEN) location points over the whole 𝐆 \mathbf{G} , back to about the level without memory, and 12.2 ∗ and 17.9 ∗ revisit points, while state and identity change by less than 1 point. Studio mentions on new-place shots fall to 6–8%. Both parts are needed: on the new-place shots of LongLive-H3 (seed 0), dropping only the backdrop sentence gains 1.9 location points (not significant), only the backdrop tokens 5.7 ∗ , and both 10.7 ∗ . Image memory without cards gains in the same way ( Tab. C1 ).
LongLive-2.0 does not copy the backdrop. It pins the first chunk of each new shot, generated after “The scene transitions.”, as the shot sink ( Sec. 2.3 ), so later chunks follow the new shot’s opening and its prompt: with the whole 𝐆 \mathbf{G} , all 111 new-place shots that receive 𝐆 \mathbf{G} alone reach their planned place (seed 0). Foreground 𝐆 \mathbf{G} there changes location, state, identity, revisit, and framing by less than 1 point and lowers same protagonist by 4.6 ∗ points ( Tab. C3 ), so LongLive-2.0 keeps the whole 𝐆 \mathbf{G} .

Cards for all injected 𝐆 \mathbf{G} / 𝐌 \mathbf{M} members raise state and identity strongly but lower location and framing, as the long cards dilute place and camera words ( Tab. 3 , framing in Appendix H ). Cards only for the entities whose name appears in the revealed prompt (string matching against the committed entity bank, 2.4 cards per shot instead of 3.9, no LLM call after the prompt, so C3 still holds) keep almost all of the gain with location and framing unchanged. Over the three seeds of Tab. 1 , they raise state by 13.9 ∗ and identity by 19.3 ∗ points over the image system.
A card reads, e.g . , “Remembered from earlier shots: Sam: Sam, a tall broad man in his mid-30s with sandy blonde hair. Current state: clothing: maroon t-shirt and grey sweatpants.” Cards follow the prompt, so the 512-token window of the text encoder, which 0.2% of prompts exceed, never cuts the user’s words. Matching takes under 1 ms, and text encoding about 0.1 s per shot with or without cards. Like the images, a card reflects memory up to shot i − 1 i{-}1 . Naive text history. To test whether cards help only because the prompt carries more text, a baseline without the agent appends, for each entity named in the prompt, the raw sentences of earlier prompts that mention it (its first mention and the two latest, about 155 words per shot). On LongLive-2.0 alone, this raises identity from 46.5% to 80.2% but costs 11.3 ∗ framing points, as old sentences bring back old camera instructions ( Tab. C4 ). With the same image memory, the agent’s cards beat the history by 5.0 ∗ state, 8.8 ∗ framing, and 4.3 ∗ revisit points: they carry the current state that the agent tracked, in a few words, instead of every earlier mention.

blocks.en:
The entity layer follows from the online setting. Views: each character and object is drawn in two views on a plain light-grey backdrop, a front view (full body for characters, the whole object for objects) and a three-quarter view. Each scene is drawn once as an empty plate, a wide view of the place without people. The three-quarter view is drawn with the front view as a reference, so both show the same entity. 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and 𝐌 \mathbf{M} are composed from the front views and the plates only, so on LongLive-2.0 the three-quarter views never reach the generator. They are used only when entity images themselves are passed as references ( Integration with LongLive-H3 ), where all views of a selected entity are listed together. Persistent versus transient (C1): entity images show only attributes that persist across shots, such as identity, clothing, dirt, damage, or assembly progress. Pose, action, and held objects stay neutral because the next prompt decides them. Memory as current belief (C1, C4): each state records its source shot and whether it was stated or inferred, and a contradicting later prompt revokes it and triggers a redraw. Refinement: a new entity is drawn from text and a changed one as an edit of its latest image, retried from its first image if the edit fails. Each entity image is checked and repaired at most once, and if it still fails, the entity keeps its previous image. Memory images are refined as in Refinement ( Appendix B ).
These choices decide what memory means when the next prompt is unknown, and they matter whenever an image would otherwise show a pose or a revoked state.

blocks.en:
The policy is Qwen3-8B with LoRA ( r = 32 r{=}32 , α = 64 \alpha{=}64 , all linear layers) and the deployed system prompt and JSON schema.
Training uses 56 stories plus 8 development stories written by Qwen3.6 (24–32 shots each) whose per-entity persistent states are accumulated by code.
RFT uses 2,865 examples (best of 4 by reward from 3,138 teacher states).
GRPO treats each shot as one decision and runs 80 steps with 8 states × \times 8 samples per step, the token-level loss of DAPO [ 80 ] , no KL term, zero-variance groups dropped, temperature 0.9, learning rate 2 × 10 − 5 2{\times}10^{-5} , gradient clipping 0.5, group standard-deviation floor 0.1, and one-step off-policy pipelining. Each seed trains on one H100 and shares rollout, judge, and image services on two 8 × \times H100 nodes (about 2–2.5 hours for three seeds in parallel).
The training judge is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and the test judge Gemini 3.8 Flash with the same prompts. They agree on 79–83% of items (per-decision correlation 0.66–0.77).

训练法官为Qune3.6-35B-A3B,测试法官为双子座 3.8 Flash,同样带有同一种提示. 他们同意79-83%的项目(每个决定的相关性为0.66-0.77)。

In Eq. 2 , the text judge scores each persistent state that the next six shots need + 1 +1 if memory holds it correctly, 0 0 if it is missing, and − 1.5 -1.5 if it is wrong.
The image term renders 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and 𝐌 \mathbf{M} with a fixed seed. Each entity of the next shot that the VLM finds recognizable and correctly drawn earns 0.51 if it is in 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and 0.49 if it is in 𝐌 \mathbf{M} (down to half if drawn in a wrong state), and each member of 𝐌 \mathbf{M} absent from the next shot costs 0.11.
These weights come from a regression of 3,867 judged entity attributes from real videos on memory composition, with story and planner fixed effects: an on-screen entity gains + 9.0 +9.0 points of state accuracy (95% CI [ 4.7 , 13.8 ] [4.7,13.8] ) in 𝐆 \mathbf{G} and + 8.7 +8.7 [ 4.6 , 12.4 ] [4.6,12.4] in the latest 𝐌 \mathbf{M} , while each absent member of 𝐌 \mathbf{M} costs − 1.9 -1.9 [ − 3.7 , 0.0 ] [-3.7,0.0] . Normalizing these effects gives 0.51, 0.49, and 0.11.

blocks.en: Appendix E Benchmark and Metrics

blocks.en:
Terse prompts are rewritten from full prompts by Gemini 3.8 Flash. The first shot is unchanged, and new places keep their description, while continuing or revisited places become one phrase (“still in”, “back in”). The protagonist and earlier entities are named without appearance or state, changes that happen in the shot remain as actions, and camera motion is kept.
Automatic checks reject rewrites that repeat attribute phrases of a character card or whose place part exceeds 15 words for continued places (at most two retries).
blocks.zh:
Terse 提示由双子座 3.8 Flash 从全提示重写. 第一个镜头没有改变,新的地点保留其描述,而继续或重新审视的地方则成为一个短语(“仍在”,“回到”)。 主角和更早的实体被命名为没有外观或状态,镜头中发生的变化仍然作为动作而保留相机运动.
自动检查拒绝重写重写字符卡的属性短语,或者其位置部分超过15个单词的继续位置(在大多数重写中).

blocks.en:
Sixteen stories with about 40 shots and 13–14 entities each (12–14 recurring, 2–4 per shot), with 7–36 returns after 5+ absent shots per story.
They are written by Gemini 3.8 Flash, a different model from the one that wrote the training stories, on topics disjoint from training, development, and hand-written stories.
Hidden states are accumulated by code from initial attributes and per-shot persistent changes.
The manifest is frozen with a hash before any method is run.

在任何方法运行之前,清单用散列冻结。

Re-judging 211 shots agrees on 95.7% (location), 94.8% (framing), and 92.3% (state items).

E1 ). These runs use a 𝐆 \mathbf{G} that also shows the current scene instead of the plain-backdrop 𝐆 \mathbf{G} of Sec. 2.3 , so their values differ slightly from Tab. 1 , but the comparison concerns the agreement of the two judges on the same shots.
Per item, they agree with Cohen’s κ \kappa 0.69–0.80 on state, identity, location, and framing, and with Spearman ρ \rho 0.66–0.73 on the pairwise ratings. Over the 14 runs, their columns correlate at r = 0.98 r=0.98 – 0.99 0.99 .
Of the 94 comparisons that were significant at seed 0 under Gemini, 87 keep their sign and significance under GPT-5.5 and none flips sign, so the gains of the full system and the entity cards do not depend on the judge. Severe artifacts are the exception ( κ \kappa 0.28), so we draw no conclusion from small artifact differences.

blocks.en:
Same protagonist fixes the shots that count from the plan: the evaluation judge reads only the hidden plan of each shot (planned camera, content, and entities present), never a video, and decides whether it shows the protagonist recognisably (face, or head and body for a non-human protagonist, but not only hands, from behind, or tiny). This holds for 349 of 857 shots (41%), with a prompt written once.
Each of these shots scores (rating − - 1)/4 against the method’s first shot of the protagonist (four frames of each shot, compared on face, hair, build, age, species, and markings, while clothing, dirt, and pose may change) and 0 if the shot judge does not see the protagonist. The reference shot itself is excluded.
Because the shots are fixed by the plan, a video that loses the protagonist or breaks down cannot score by showing the protagonist less often, and because pairs at any place and distance count, carrying the previous shot’s pixels forward does not help either. Revisit rates whether a returning shot shows the same place as the last visit and counts a return only if both shots are judged to be at their planned location, as the geometric place consistency of StoryEngine [ 60 ] counts only shots in the right scene, so a model that stays in one place cannot score by looking the same.

blocks.en:
MIR follows StoryEngine exactly (its App. D.8). It takes four evenly spaced frames per shot, including the first and last, and keeps InsightFace buffalo_l detections at 640 × \times 640 with score ≥ \geq 0.55. In shot order, each embedding joins the cluster with the most similar mean if the cosine is ≥ \geq 0.45 and otherwise starts a new one, and single-detection clusters are dropped. MIR is the minimum over clusters of the mean cosine between detections from different shots, and 0 when no cluster spans two shots.
We report MIR here rather than in Tab. 1 because it measures faces only (two of our 25 protagonists are an animal and a robot), it rewards videos that repeat nearly the same frames across shots, and it does not penalize a video that breaks down (Self-Forcing 0.400). Same protagonist is used in the main paper.
With our memory, MIR is higher on both MiniMax-H3 generators ( Tab. E3 ): by + 0.005 +0.005 (RAVEN) and + 0.049 +0.049 (LongLive-H3) over the 25 stories, and by + 0.051 +0.051 and + 0.070 +0.070 on the nine hand-written stories, though none of these differences is significant. Among StoryMem, StoryEngine, and our offline variants, the offline variant on H3 Ref2VA has the highest MIR (0.403 and 0.455, against 0.385 and 0.423 for StoryEngine).
On LongLive-2.0, image memory lowers MIR from 0.334 to 0.191. LongLive-2.0’s built-in memory carries the previous shot’s K/V and so keeps some faces across adjacent shots, which MIR rewards. ArcFace embeddings of small generated faces are also noisy (cosine 0.1–0.3 between faces of the same shot below 60 px, 0.6–0.8 above 100 px), which lowers MIR for every model at these resolutions.

blocks.en:
Rolling Forcing supports a single prompt, so we split generation per shot, re-cache KV at prompt switches as in LongLive [ 74 ] , and wrap RoPE after 1,024 positions (stories reach 1,764 latent frames). It takes 19.3 s per shot.
The other Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B models use the same protocol: one continuous rollout per story, 42 latent frames per shot (10.3–10.5 s at 16 fps), only the current shot prompt, and one seed set before the first shot. Shot 0 of every model is identical to its official inference. Self-Forcing uses the official sampler (4 steps, 3-frame blocks) with the repository’s rolling KV cache of 21 frames (its training context) and no sink. Cached frames are recomputed under each new prompt as for Rolling Forcing, and RoPE wraps after 1,024 frames (18.2 s per shot). Causal-Forcing is run with the authors’ long-video checkpoint, which uses the Rolling Forcing inference code (17.4 s per shot). Its 5-second chunkwise checkpoint, run like Self-Forcing, breaks down within about two shots (87.6% of its shots have severe artifacts). CausVid uses the repository’s long-video script, with rollouts of up to 21 latent frames, each started from 3 overlap frames, and 3 steps. Rollouts never cross a shot boundary, so a new prompt starts the next rollout and re-encodes the overlap under that prompt (13.4 s per shot). SkyReels-V2 uses DF-1.3B-540P at 960 × \times 544 with official settings (30 steps, guidance 6, TeaCache 0.3): shot 0 is text-to-video and each later shot is a video extension of 160 frames (10 s at 16 fps) conditioned on the last 17 frames, with its own prompt (87.6 s per shot, one seed).
As it is far from real time, its results are in Tab. F1 rather than in Tab. 1 : it is below LongLive-2.0 with its built-in memory in state, location, and revisit, slightly above it in identity and same protagonist, and has the lowest imaging quality of all methods.
All times are measured on one H100 (mean over 15 shots after a warm-up, FlashAttention-2, no compilation) and include decoding. The videos themselves were generated on A100s, and the same timing scripts run on an A100 match the generation times within 1–3%.
Self-Forcing and the chunkwise Causal-Forcing model degrade once the first frames leave the cache, as in their official single-prompt code, so their judge metrics should be read together with the artifact rate.

blocks.en:
StoryMem [ 83 ] keeps keyframe memory in Wan2.2-A14B and runs with its official setting (5.06 s shots, offloading on one H100). StoryEngine [ 60 ] is an agent system on our Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone, run under our protocol: Gemini 3.8 Flash [ 18 ] plans, GPT Image [ 48 ] draws keyframes, and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B generates 6 s shots. Prompts are revealed one at a time, and its video repair and best-of- N N selection are disabled. Ours offline swaps in the API agent (Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT Image) with synchronous refinement and generates either with H3 Ref2VA (50 steps, up to six references) or with Wan2.2-TI2V-5B image-to-video at StoryEngine’s settings (1280 × \times 704, 145 frames at 24 fps, 50 steps, guidance 5, shift 5). For Wan, GPT Image draws a keyframe from the same references and rewritten prompt, and the shot description becomes the text prompt. Unlike StoryEngine, the previous shot’s last frame is not used.
These systems spend 28–114 × \times more time per second of video than our real-time system ( Tab. F2 ).
On the same Wan2.2-5B backbone and keyframe model, our offline variant beats StoryEngine by 9.3 ∗ state points, ties it in identity, same protagonist, and location, and is 1.7 × \times faster per shot. StoryEngine leads in revisit ( + 15.7 +15.7 ∗ ) and slightly in imaging: it anchors every recurring place to a panorama and starts a shot from the previous shot’s last frame when they fit, whereas we keep one plate per place and draw every keyframe afresh.
With H3 Ref2VA, the same offline memory reaches about the same state and identity and has the fewest severe artifacts of these systems (0.5%).
Rolling Forcing, StoryMem, and StoryEngine are released for research or non-commercial use. SkyReels-V2, StoryMem, StoryEngine, and the offline variants use one seed because of cost.

blocks.en:
Does memory hurt the base model when nothing needs remembering?
On 42 prompts of VBench (every sixth of the standard list), each generated for about 64 s as six shots of the same prompt with the image system, against LongLive-2.0’s official single-prompt rollout (seed 0, VBench-Long protocol with 2 s clips), subject, background, and motion consistency are unchanged ( − 0.4 -0.4 , + 0.2 +0.2 , and + 0.0 +0.0 points), aesthetic and imaging quality rise ( + 5.0 +5.0 ∗ and + 3.5 +3.5 ∗ ) because they do not decay over the minute, and dynamic degree falls by 7.5 (not significant).
The small consistency losses come only from clips that straddle one of our 10.5 s shot boundaries, and LongLive-2.0’s own multi-shot mode with the same prompt loses as much dynamic degree ( − 6.2 -6.2 ∗ ), so they come from cutting into shots rather than from memory.

LongLive-2.0自己的多发射击模式同样会失去动态度(−6.2-6.2 *), 因此它们来自切入镜头而非记忆。

blocks.en:
In robot videos, a camera that stays near an object, or a closed container, hides things that must later come back. Here the memory pictures are frames that the camera has already observed, or crops of them, so no image model is used ( Tab. G1 ).
The robot video model of Long-WAM [ 27 ] (Robot-M) is LongLive-2.0 trained further on robot and egocentric videos. We run it as released, with a rolling KV cache of about 10.5 s and no sink.
From each of the seven first frames that ship with it, we synthesize a wrist-camera observation (a 2.5 s zoom to the task’s target object, then a close-up, 13.2 s in total) and write it into the cache, so the window holds only the close-up.
The model then continues for 5.3 s under the instruction followed by “the camera moves back and the whole scene is visible again.”
Our memory is built from the first frame before the close-up: the 35B model of the main text names the target object, returns its box, and writes a card of at most 20 words. The first frame and a crop around the box enter the sink as still blocks, and the card is appended to the prompt.
Without memory, the model turns to a different scene. With our memory, the object is back in 96.4% of the last frames (60.7% without), and the same-object score rises by 2.36 ∗ points, in all seven scenes.
Given the same observation, pictures, and card as references, the offline MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA (50 steps) keeps the object even without memory but continues into a different room. Our memory restores the scene (scene consistency from 2.9 to 7.0 of 10, + 4.1 +4.1 ∗ ) and raises the same-object score by 1.36 ∗ points.
blocks.zh:
在机器人视频中,一个停留在物体附近的相机,或者一个被关闭的容器,隐藏了以后必须回来的东西. 这里的内存图片是相机已经观测到的帧,或者它们的收成,因此没有使用图像模型(Tab. G1.).
Long-WAM [27] (Robot-M)的机器人视频模型是LongLive-2.0,在机器人和以自我为中心的视频方面受到进一步培训. 我们运行它作为发布, 一个滚动的KV缓存 大约10.5 s,没有水槽。
从第一个七个框架中,我们用它来合成一个手腕-相机观察(一个2.5 s放大到任务的目标对象,然后是特写,总共13.2 s),并写入缓存中,所以窗口只保留特写.
然后,该型号在指令下继续5.3 s,然后是“相机向后移动,整个场景再次可见。 “
我们的记忆是从特写前的第一个框架所构建的:主文本的35B模型取出目标对象的名字,还原其盒子,并写出一张最多为20个字的卡片. 第一个相框和一个相框周围的收成作为静止的块入入水槽,卡片被附在提示上.
没有记忆,模型会变成不同的场景. 有了我们的记忆,这个物体回到了96.4%的上个帧(60.7%没有),同个对象的分数上升了2.36分*,在所有七个场景中.
考虑到与参考文献相同的观察,图片,和卡片,离线的MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA(50个步骤)即使没有内存也保留了对象,但继续进入不同的房间. 我们的记忆恢复了场景(场景一致性从 2.9 到 7.0的10,+ 4.1 + 4.1 *),将同对象分数提高1.36分.

blocks.en:
Generated robot data needs long videos in which the robot works through many steps while parts of the scene leave the view and come back.
We take the first frames of 30 validation clips of RoVid-X [ 14 ] , which cover one and two arms, grippers and hands, and head-mounted and fixed cameras.
For each first frame, Gemini 3.8 Flash drafted a script of eight 8 s instructions (64 s in total), which we then edited by hand.
The first instructions finish the clip’s own task. Each script then hides one or two things and brings each back one to four instructions later. A head camera turns away and back (20 return moments), or a drawer, fridge, box, or lid is closed and reopened, or an object is covered and uncovered (21 moments).
An instruction that brings something back never describes it, for example “pull the top left drawer open again and reach in for what you put there,” so only memory can tell the generator what to show.
Each segment continues from the last frame of the previous one, so that the 64 s video is meant to be one continuous take, although the generator can still cut on its own. Without memory, this frame is all that the generator knows about the scene.
Unlike the main text, where the memory for a shot must be ready before its prompt arrives (C1), each instruction here is available one segment before it plays, as in a scripted robot task, and the agent uses it to choose pictures and rewrite it. This section therefore tests observation-based memory on robot videos, not C1.
blocks.zh:
所生成的机器人数据需要长相的视频,其中机器人通过多步来工作,而部分场景则会离开取景并返回.
我们拍摄了30个验证片段的第一帧 罗维德X[14], 覆盖了一和两只手臂, 抓手和手, 以及头架和固定相机。
每个第一帧,双子座 3.8 Flash起草了由8个8个指令(共64 s)组成的脚本,然后我们用手进行编辑.
第一个指令完成剪辑本身的任务。 每部剧本再隐藏一到两件事情,并在后期将每件剧本带回一到四个指令. 头相机转而回转(20回分秒),或抽屉,冰箱,盒子,或盖子被关闭并重新打开,或物体被覆盖并被揭开(21回分秒).
一个带回东西的指示从来没有描述过它,例如“把左上方的抽屉再次打开并伸入你放在那里的东西”,因此只有记忆才能告诉生成者要显示什么。
每段从上段的最后一帧延续,因此64 s的视频本意是一个连续取景,尽管发电机仍然可以自行剪接. 没有记忆,这个相框就是发电机所知道的场景的全部.
与正文不同的是:一出镜头的内存必须在出场前准备好(C1),这里的每个指令在出场前都有一个段,如同在被脚本化的机器人任务中一样,代理使用它来选择相片并重写. 因此本节在机器人视频上测试基于观测的内存,而不是C1.

blocks.en:
Unlike the open-loop agent of the main text, this agent observes the video, because a robot acts in one continuous scene rather than in separate shots. Where an object ends up, or whether a drawer is still open, depends on the generated video rather than on the script, so the memory has to be read from that video. As in the close-up test, it is an observation-based variant: its memory pictures are frames that the robot’s camera has already shown, or crops of them, so it needs no image model.
After each segment, the agent looks at three of its frames. It describes the view, lists the visible objects with their position and look, and records whether each container is open or closed and what it holds. It also picks a frame to keep, a frame that shows the inside of an open container, and boxes for up to two objects.
Code turns these observations into two parts of memory. A record of objects and containers keeps an object that was put into a closed container as hidden inside it. A bank of pictures holds one view per segment, container interiors, and the newest crop of each object, each with a caption and the segment it comes from.
Before each segment, a router answers one narrow question about the next instruction: does something come back into view, because the camera turns back, a container is reopened, a cover is lifted, or an object is taken out? It agrees with the scripts’ annotations in 188 of 210 segments.
Only when something comes back, the agent sees the bank as thumbnails and lists every picture of the returning place, container, or object. It pins the newest matching view and the newest close view (at most two pictures, Fig. G1 ) and rewrites the instruction so that it names what comes back and how it looked when last seen.
Otherwise it pins nothing and only rewrites the instruction to name the objects with their look.
Pinning only on returns matters: pictures pinned in almost every segment make the generator restore old states, for example a tube put into a drawer reappears on the cabinet.
The agent was developed on one of the 30 episodes and then kept fixed for all runs.
blocks.zh:
与正文的开放代理不同,这名代理观察了视频,因为一个机器人在一个连续的场景中进行动作,而不是单独拍摄. 如果一个物体最后,或者抽屉是否仍然打开,则取决于生成的视频而不是脚本,所以内存必须从该视频读取. 和特写测试一样,这是一个基于观察的变体:它的内存图片是机器人相机已经显示的帧,或者它们的收成,所以不需要图像模型.
每段后,代理查看其三帧. 它描述视图,列出可见物体及其位置和外观,并记录每个容器是打开还是关闭,以及它持有什么. 它还会选取一个框来保存,一个框来显示一个打开的容器的内侧,以及最多两个物体的盒子.
代码将这些观察变成记忆的两个部分. 物体和容器的记录将一个被放入封闭容器的物体藏在其中。 一个图片库每个部分有一个视图,容器内部,以及每个物体的最新收成,每个部分都有一个标题和它来自的部分。
在每一段之前,一个路由器回答了关于下个指令的一个狭义问题:有什么东西重新出现,因为相机回转,一个容器被重新打开,一个封面被解除,或者一个物体被取出? 它同意210个部分中的188个部分的文字说明。
只有当有东西回来时,代理商将银行视为缩略图并列出返回地的每一个相片,容器,或物品. 它将最新的相配视图和最新的相近视图(在大多数两个相片上是Fig. G1)钉上并重写了指令,这样它就可以命名回回回出现的内容以及上次看到时的外观.
否则它会针入一无所有,只会重写指示,用外观来命名对象.
固定在返回事项上:几乎每段被钉住的相片使生成器恢复了旧状态,例如,放在抽屉中的管子重新出现在柜上。
该代理机是在30集的一集上被开发出来的,后被固定用于所有运行.

blocks.en:
Table G2 uses two generators from earlier sections: FastH3-Omni, as in the real-time runs of Appendix B , and H3 Ref2VA, as in the offline variant of Appendix F .
In the real-time system, FastH3-Omni [ 16 ] (8 steps) generates each segment, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [ 52 ] runs the agent. The pinned pictures and then the latest frame enter the sink, and the new segment starts from the latest frame. A fixed preamble of the prompt says that the earlier pictures were recorded in the same video, names what each one shows, and states that the target continues from the latest frame without a cut.
While segment i − 1 i{-}1 renders, the agent observes segment i − 2 i{-}2 and prepares segment i i from instruction i i . The quality runs used A100 GPUs.
In the offline system, MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [ 45 ] (50 steps) generates each segment with the pinned pictures and the latest frame as references, and Gemini 3.8 Flash runs the agent. It observes segment i − 1 i{-}1 before segment i i renders and crops objects with Grounding DINO [ 42 ] boxes for their names.
The original model receives the latest frame and the user’s instruction in the same layout. Both arms share the first segment and use the same seed for every later segment. The second-seed run changes the seeds after the first segment.

blocks.en:
The closed loop still runs in parallel with generation. The agent observes decoded frames and writes memory while the generator renders on other GPUs, and this memory enters only when the next segment starts, never within a segment. How early the agent can observe depends on the generator. FastH3-Omni is bidirectional and returns a segment only when all of it is decoded, so when segment i i starts, the newest frame that the agent has seen is 8 s old. LongLive-H3 generates a segment chunk by chunk and decodes each chunk as it is generated, so the agent can observe the first half of segment i − 1 i{-}1 while the second half is still being generated, and the newest frame it has seen is 4 s old.
We timed both loops on six episodes, with the generator on eight B200 GPUs and the agent on two A100 GPUs. With FastH3-Omni, the agent (2.3 s on average) never makes the generator wait. With the last decoded frame passed straight to the next request, each 8 s segment takes 7.6 s on average, and every segment is ready before it is due to play. With LongLive-H3 on five of the GPUs, the first half of a segment is decoded 3.3 s after the segment starts and the agent needs 1.9 s, so the generator usually waits about 0.5 s for it at the boundary. The loop still runs in real time, at 5.8 s per 8 s segment on average (at most 7.7 s), because generation is faster than playback. We time LongLive-H3 but do not score it. It is not trained on robot videos, and with or without memory it does not keep the input robot, whose grippers, for example, turn into humanoid hands early in the video.
blocks.zh:
闭环仍然与生成平行运行. 代理机在生成器在其他GPU上制作时观察解码帧并写入内存,这个内存只有在下段开始时才进入,从不在一个段内. 剂能观察到的多快取决于生成器. FastH3-Omni是双向的,只有在全部解码后才会返回一段,因此当一段i开始时,代理机看到的最新框架是8 s 旧. LongLive-H3通过块来生成一段块并解码每个块所生成的块,这样,代理可以观察到一段的上半部 I− 1 i{}1 而后半部仍在生成中,它看到的最新框架是4 s 旧.
我们为六集的时间设定了两个循环,其中8个B200GPU的生成器和两个A100GPU的代理. 与FastH3-Omni相伴而来,代理(平均2.3 s)从未让发电机等待. 随着上个解码框被直接传递到下个请求中,每个8个分块平均取7.6个分块,每个分块在预定播放前都准备好了. 随着LongLive-H3在5个GPU上,一段的上半段在段开始后被解码为3.3 s,代理机需要1.9 s,因此生成器通常在边界上等待约0.5 s. 循环仍然实时运行,平均为每8个段5.8 s (最多为7.7 s),因为生成速度快于回放. 我们给LongLive-H3计时,但不要得分。 它没有在机器人视频上接受训练,无论是否有记忆,它都不保留输入机器人,例如,其抓取器在视频早期会变成人手.

blocks.en:
Table G2 compares whole 64 s videos at the 41 return moments and over all 210 generated segments.
Our memory raises the consistency of what comes back with its last appearance from 3.98 to 5.59 with FastH3-Omni ( + 1.61 +1.61 ∗ , a second seed + 1.66 +1.66 ∗ ) and from 3.54 to 5.51 with H3 Ref2VA ( + 1.98 +1.98 ∗ ).
The hidden thing is back in view at 76% instead of 44% of the return moments with FastH3-Omni, and back with the same identity and position at 56% instead of 20% (H3 Ref2VA: 44% instead of 5%).
Camera returns gain the most ( + 2.55 +2.55 ∗ and + 2.35 +2.35 ∗ ), because the pinned view shows the whole place. Reopened containers gain less ( + 0.71 +0.71 , not significant, and + 1.62 +1.62 ∗ ): in four of the nine FastH3-Omni reopenings that score below 5, the generator never opens the lid, lifts the cover, or takes the object out, which memory cannot fix.
Task progress stays level (neither difference significant), and segments in which nothing comes back revert to an earlier state about as often as without memory, because nothing is pinned there.
The pinned views also show the robot, so its look stays closer to the input image (same-robot score 7.84 vs . 7.05 ∗ with FastH3-Omni and 7.36 vs . 6.53 ∗ with H3 Ref2VA). Figure G1 shows four return moments.
blocks.zh:
表G2比较了整个64 s视频在41回放时段和所有210回放时段.

blocks.en:
The remaining failures fall into three groups.
First, the stored picture can be wrong. The agent sees only three frames per segment, so in one drawer episode it kept the interior from before the tube was put in and pinned that picture at the reopening.
Second, the generator can follow a pinned picture too literally. When the pinned view shows an earlier open state, FastH3-Omni may briefly reopen a lid that was closed, and it sometimes jumps to the pinned frame instead of turning toward it.
Third, the robot itself drifts slowly over the minute, for example from a gripper to a hand. With memory, its identity score is at most 5 in 21.9% of segment ends (30.5% without memory).

第三,机器人本身在瞬间缓慢地漂移,例如从抓手到手. 在有内存的情况下,其身份分数最多为21.9%分之5(30.5%无内存).

blocks.en:
Memory follows the story up to the previous prompt, because it is built before the next prompt arrives (C3). Two cases follow from this.
A persistent change that the current prompt states for the first time, such as a character shaving, is not yet in the memory images of that shot, which can keep the earlier look until the agent has drawn the change for the following shots.
A recalled place comes with the picture of its last visit. If a character has changed since, the cards state the new look, but an attribute that no card names can follow the earlier picture until the place is drawn again.
Re-injecting updated memory within a shot, once its prompt has arrived, would address both cases and is left to future work.

一旦迅速到达,在镜头中重新注入更新的内存将处理这两个案件,并留给今后的工作。

Framing. For every shot, the judge also decides whether the shot size, camera angle, and main subject agree with the planned camera and content ( framing_match in the judge prompt of Appendix E ). Re-judging agrees on 94.8% of shots, and the second judge agrees with κ = 0.71 \kappa=0.71 . None of the compared works scores framing.
On LongLive-2.0, framing rises with our full system from 58.5% to 65.9% of shots (three seeds), but planned close-ups, a quarter of all shots, fall from 75.5% to 63.7%. Memory images show whole entities in medium or wide views and pull the generator toward that shot size, so 78% of the remaining misses are rendered as medium shots.
Memory is built before the prompt (C3), so it cannot be drawn at the shot size of the coming shot, whereas StoryEngine and our offline variants, which draw a keyframe or references after each prompt, reach 74–95% framing.
Long text also competes with camera words: cards for every injected member cost 22.4 ∗ framing points alone and 11.9 ∗ with images, whereas cards for the entities that the prompt names cost none ( − 0.7 -0.7 with the 35B planner, not significant).

Other limitations. Memory images can also pull some scene changes toward the previous place. Generators that attend to them in every chunk, such as MiniMax-H3, are affected most: with the whole 𝐆 \mathbf{G} they lose moves to new places, which foreground 𝐆 \mathbf{G} restores ( Tab. C3 ).
On MiniMax-H3, memory K/V also depend on the prompt and cannot be prefilled before it arrives ( Sec. 3.3 ).
Real time on LongLive-H3 needs five B200s for generation. On H100 it needs eight, and an H100 agent delivers most updates one shot late ( Appendix B ).
The judge compares shots with text descriptions, which may favor entity cards, but same protagonist, which compares two shots, also rises with cards.

We report the share of best-version votes: a version chosen alone receives one vote, tied versions share it, Cannot judge answers (11 of 1,280) are left out, and shares are averaged over the 25 stories. The 95% intervals are percentiles of 4,000 bootstrap draws that resample participants and stories independently.
On LongLive-2.0, against its built-in memory, our full system receives 98.8% [ 95.7,100 ] [95.7,100] of the votes for persistent state, 100% for identity, 93.8% for location, and 100% for visual quality.
On LongLive-H3, in the three-way choice, it receives 97.8% [ 93.2,100 ] [93.2,100] for persistent state, 96.4% for identity, and 94.0% for location, while K/V carried across shots receives at most 1.3% on any criterion.
Visual quality on LongLive-H3 is split between independent shots (55.1%) and ours (43.6%), a difference of − 11.4 -11.4 points with a 95% interval of [ − 31.3 , 9.4 ] [-31.3,9.4] , and more than half of these answers are ties.
It covers four shots per story and one seed, with a convenience sample and incomplete counterbalancing (21 of 30 layouts), so it complements rather than calibrates the automated metrics.
